I take women’s rights seriously, so this is one of the first things I asked about while visiting Ghardaïa, Algeria  Now this is not necessarily for any reason. It has nothing to do with religion or location. The only thing it has to do with is that many communities that are small and follow old traditions typically give less rights and protections to women. However, I was pleasantly surprised that this is not the case in Ghardaia.   I really appreciate what I learned about  Mozabite communities, giving women in their own committees and ability to make decisions for themselves. When it comes to dress, extra protections, to feel safe and comfortable in their marriages, and the community standing in solidarity with its women. videos.caption: Algeria achieved sovereignty in 1962 following an eight-year armed conflict that ended 132 years of French colonial rule. After the 1830 conquest, France organized the territory as integral departments rather than a protectorate, establishing a hierarchy where European settlers held political dominance over the disenfranchised Muslim majority. Inequality under the Code de l'Indigénat and the violent suppression of nationalist demonstrations at Sétif in May 1945 convinced Algerian leaders that electoral reform was unviable. On November 1, 1954, the National Liberation Front (FLN) launched an armed insurrection against French targets. The conflict expanded into protracted guerrilla warfare, urban clashes during the 1957 Battle of Algiers, and extensive French counterinsurgency campaigns involving forced population transfers and torture. Diplomatic pressure orchestrated by the FLN abroad, coupled with domestic instability, triggered the collapse of France's Fourth Republic in 1958 and returned Charles de Gaulle to power. De Gaulle recognized the political impossibility of retaining Algeria and opened negotiations that produced the Évian Accords in March 1962. On July 1, 1962, a national referendum resulted in an overwhelming vote for independence, recognized by France on July 3 and declared by Algeria on July 5. The outcome spurred the flight of nearly one million European settlers (pieds-noirs) and left the new state to confront substantial economic disruption and political consolidation. https://f.mtr.cool/u6dj3dqcba https://f.mtr.cool/olmi66dkva
